clinicalPearls: A hereditary connective-tissue (collagenopathy) disorder in which hearing loss is one component alongside ocular, orofacial and skeletal features
Hearing loss may be sensorineural, conductive from middle-ear disease, or mixed, and is often high-frequency
Caused by mutations in collagen genes including COL2A1, COL11A1 and COL11A2; most subtypes are autosomal dominant
The COL11A2 subtype (type 3) shows the syndrome's systemic features with hearing loss but without the ocular involvement
Cleft palate or a Pierre Robin sequence contributes to conductive hearing loss through Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent middle-ear effusion
The associated high myopia carries a significant risk of retinal detachment, so ophthalmology assessment is essential
A child with cleft palate, midface hypoplasia and hearing loss should be assessed for Stickler syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Stickler syndrome is caused by mutations in genes encoding types II and XI collagen, which are important structural components of cartilage, the vitreous of the eye and the connective tissue of the inner and middle ear. Defective collagen impairs the integrity of these tissues, producing the characteristic vitreoretinal degeneration and myopia, orofacial abnormalities such as cleft palate and midface underdevelopment, joint and skeletal problems, and hearing loss. Middle-ear collagen abnormality and Eustachian tube dysfunction related to palatal clefting contribute a conductive element, while cochlear collagen involvement contributes a sensorineural element, giving frequently mixed hearing loss.
additionalDifferentials: Marshall syndrome with overlapping facial and sensory features
Other syndromic hearing loss such as branchio-oto-renal or Waardenburg syndrome
Isolated cleft palate or Pierre Robin sequence with secondary otitis media with effusion
Other inherited collagenopathies affecting connective tissue
Isolated high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration
Non-syndromic mixed hearing loss from chronic middle-ear disease
additionalInvestigations: Audiometry with tympanometry to distinguish conductive, sensorineural and mixed loss
Ophthalmic assessment for high myopia, vitreous abnormality and retinal detachment risk
Examination of the palate and airway for clefting and Robin sequence
Skeletal and joint assessment for features of the associated arthropathy
Molecular genetic testing of collagen genes to confirm the subtype
redFlags: Sudden visual symptoms suggesting retinal detachment in a highly myopic patient
Airway compromise in an infant with Pierre Robin sequence
Progressive hearing loss impairing speech and language development
Recurrent middle-ear effusions causing persistent conductive loss
reference.prognosis: Hearing loss is usually mild to moderate and manageable with amplification or middle-ear treatment, but the main threats to long-term outcome are sight-threatening retinal detachment and, in infancy, airway compromise from Robin sequence; overall prognosis is good with coordinated multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Managing recurrent middle-ear effusion without recognising an underlying syndrome
Failing to arrange retinal-detachment prophylaxis and surveillance in high myopia
Assuming hearing loss is purely conductive and missing a sensorineural component
Overlooking the diagnosis in the ocular-sparing COL11A2 subtype
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
